## 1. Learning Outcome

By the end of this hands-on exercise, I will be able to:

-   import an aspatial data file into R,
-   convert it into a simple point feature data frame by using the appropriate coordinate system, and
-   plot interactive proportional symbol maps using the **tmap** package.

## 2. Getting Started

### 2.1 Installing and Loading R Packages

The R packages required for this exercise are: **sf**, **tmap**, and **tidyverse**. The code chunk below uses `pacman::p_load()` to check, install, and load all the necessary packages.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)
```

## 3. Geospatial Data Wrangling

### 3.1 The Data

The data set used in this hands-on exercise is *SGPools_svy21.csv*. It is a csv file that consists of 306 observations and 7 variables. The seven variables are: `NAME`, `ADDRESS`, `POSTCODE`, `XCOORD`, `YCOORD`, `OUTLET TYPE`, and `Gp1Gp2 Winnings`. The `XCOORD` and `YCOORD` columns are in the Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinate System (EPSG: 3414).

Figure below shows the first 15 records of SGPools_svy21.csv. It consists of seven columns. The XCOORD and YCOORD columns are the x-coordinates and y-coordinates of SingPools outlets and branches. They are in [Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinates System](https://www.sla.gov.sg/sirent/CoordinateSystems.aspx).

![](https://r4va.netlify.app/chap22/img/image1.jpg)

### 3.2 Importing the Data

The code chunk below uses `read_csv()` of the **readr** package to import *SGPools_svy21.csv* into R as a tibble data frame called `sgpools`.

```{r}
sgpools <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W9/SGPools_svy21.csv")
```

After importing the data file, it is important to examine whether the data has been imported correctly.

```{r}
list(sgpools)
```

Notice that the `sgpools` data in tibble data frame format contains 306 rows and 7 columns. The `XCOORD` and `YCOORD` are currently stored as numeric values and therefore not yet recognised as geographic coordinates.

### 3.3 Creating a Simple Feature Data Frame from an Aspatial Data Frame

The code chunk below converts `sgpools` into a simple feature data frame by using `st_as_sf()` of the **sf** package.

```{r}
sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(sgpools,
                       coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
                       crs = 3414)
```

::: callout-note
-   The `coords` argument requires the column name of the x-coordinates first, followed by the column name of the y-coordinates.
-   The `crs` argument requires the coordinates system in EPSG format. EPSG: 3414 is the Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinate System. You can search for other countries' EPSG codes at [epsg.io](https://epsg.io/).
:::

Figure below shows the data table of *sgpools_sf*. Notice that a new column called geometry has been added into the data frame.

![](https://r4va.netlify.app/chap22/img/image2.jpg)

The code chunk below is used to display the basic information of the newly created `sgpools_sf` simple feature data frame.

```{r}
print(sgpools_sf)
```

Notice that the output shows the data is now in simple feature point geometry format. The `XCOORD` and `YCOORD` columns have been replaced by a single `geometry` column.

## 4. Drawing Proportional Symbol Maps

To create an interactive proportional symbol map in R, the view mode of **tmap** will be used.

The code chunk below turns on the interactive mode of **tmap**.

```{r}
tmap_mode("view")
```

### 4.1 Creating an Interactive Point Symbol Map

The code chunk below is used to create an interactive point symbol map.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = 1,
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)
```

### 4.2 Making the Proportional Symbol Map

To draw a proportional symbol map, I need to assign a numerical variable to the `size` argument of `tm_bubbles()`. The size of each bubble will then be proportional to the value of the selected variable.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)
```

::: callout-note
It is easy to see that the larger the `Gp1Gp2 Winnings` amount, the bigger the bubble on the map.
:::

### 4.3 Using Fill to Differentiate Between Outlet Types

The `fill` argument can be used to encode a categorical variable with colour. In the code chunk below, `OUTLET TYPE` is mapped to `fill` to differentiate between branch types.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)
```

### 4.4 Synchronised Small Multiple Maps with tm_facets()

An impressive and useful feature of **tmap** is that it allows a faceted map to be created in view mode, whereby the coordinated view is enabled by default. The `sync` argument in `tm_facets()` is used to produce multiple maps with synchronised zoom and pan settings.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) +
  tm_facets(by = "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)
```

::: callout-note
Before creating the faceted map shown above, `tmap_mode("view")` must be called to activate the interactive viewing mode.
:::

The code chunk below switches tmap back to the static plot mode.

```{r}
tmap_mode("plot")
```
